goals.statement: Every dollar this studio spends is written down somewhere a machine can add up.
goals.statement_short: nothing adds up what this studio has spent
goals.why_it_matters: The ledger's own arithmetic is good — the missing thing was records. The last balance anyone wrote down is $1.858 on 2026-08-31; $0.59 has been spent since with no balance recorded, two runs carry no price at all, and the original credit purchase — the actual cash — is recorded nowhere. One reading of the vendor's real balance closes the tail.

path_to_green.narrative: The record is backfilled from the ledger and the pipeline appends as it spends; the remaining step is spend estimates on tier-2 cards.

goals.statement: Every asset in the build has a written record of its origin, its terms, and its cost.
goals.statement_short: a sound in the game has no record of where it came from
goals.why_it_matters: One sound file is in the build with nothing anywhere saying who made it, what its terms are, or what it cost. That is not a small bookkeeping gap: an asset whose rights nobody has established is the kind of unknown that stops a public release, and it stays invisible until somebody looks.

goals.statement: Every credential this studio depends on is present on the machine that needs it.
goals.statement_short: a credential this studio depends on is missing from this machine
goals.why_it_matters: You work from two machines, and a key that exists on only one is a machine that cannot do the work. Key names are compared against what .env.example declares; the value is dropped at the split and never read, stored or shown.

path_to_green.narrative: Copy the missing name into this machine's .env from wherever the key is kept.

escalates.because: Only you hold these; nobody in the studio can put a key on your machine for you.

goals.statement: We can say what the studio's largest recurring cost is doing over time.
goals.statement_short: nothing records the model budget's history
goals.why_it_matters: The model budget is by a wide margin the largest ongoing expense here — far more than the $2.23 of art this pillar reports carefully. HQ already detects when the window runs dry and parks the work that was waiting, so the events happen; hq/data/outbox/_limit.json is simply overwritten each time. One append instead of one overwrite and the studio's real cost curve exists. Until then, the only spend Finance can talk about is the small one.

measure.label: limit events are appended to a history, not overwritten
measure.says_true: every window outage and recovery is appended to hq/data/history/limits.jsonl
measure.says_false: limit events are overwritten, so the cost has no history

path_to_green.narrative: Recording is in; the first chart draws itself as events accumulate.

goals.statement: When the game starts needing words, they can be translated without going back over the code.
goals.statement_short: there is no translation plumbing, so every word added now is a retrofit later
goals.why_it_matters: The game starts almost wordless and gains text as it gets technical — S-7 binds phase 1's farming loop, not the whole arc, and programmable bots will need words by design. So text is coming on purpose. There is no i18n here at all: no tr(), no locale setting, no translation files. Every string written before the plumbing exists is one somebody has to go back and find. This is the cheapest it will ever be to fix, and it gets more expensive with each phase.

measure.label: the project has translation plumbing
measure.says_false: the project declares no translations, and nothing in the code calls tr()

path_to_green.narrative: Put the plumbing in before the words arrive, not after. Phase 2's machines are where text starts, so this wants doing before them.
